section.title: Scope quickly enough to learn, and concretely enough to get feedback
section.deck: Boris Cherny recalls planning a rapidly expanding organization and using parallel designs to expose risk.

blocks.question: How can one person scope projects for hundreds of engineers?
answer: Cherny describes a period when Facebook Groups grew from roughly 150–200 people to roughly 600–800 as leadership invested in a communities strategy. Executive support created resources quickly, and technical leads then had to decide what those engineers would actually build. He repeatedly produced rough scoping documents that compared several technical options and matched an approximate team size to the selected approach.

In hindsight, he would have added fewer people at first. He thinks the important work was solving people’s problems and finding product fit, then gradually increasing investment. Headcount could not create that learning all at once. The distinction is between an executive’s capacity to fund a priority and the product team’s need to discover a good direction.

For a particularly large migration merging group and page data models, the problem spanned product, integrity, advertising, and data layers. Rather than wait indefinitely for a decision, Cherny gathered technical leads, divided them into two teams, and gave both the same requirements and roughly three hours to design a solution. The independently produced designs were about 80 percent alike. Their shared core offered a direction for execution; the differences made the uncertainty visible and suggested targeted technical spikes.
blocks.speaker: Boris Cherny

blocks.question: How did people react to the internal design competition?
answer: Cherny says it was an unusual idea and he largely acted by scheduling the session. The unclear path required action, but because he did not already know the answer, it also required gathering people to build agreement. He treats leadership as balancing those two modes: sometimes a leader must create the conditions for a decision instead of first obtaining consensus on every part of the process.
blocks.speaker: Boris Cherny

blocks.question: What advice would you give a technical lead who needs to scope work quickly?
answer: His main warning is spending too long in details. Start at a high level and time-box a rough plan—he suggests about 30 minutes for an initial pass, or a couple of hours when the code needs investigation. Scoping cannot eliminate every detail before work begins.

Find the experts and present a straw-man design rather than only asking an open-ended question. A concrete proposal gives them something to correct. He also says the AI tools available in his interview context could help explore a codebase and identify systems involved, a task that previously demanded more manual investigation. That tool example is part of his account, not a requirement to adopt a particular product.
blocks.speaker: Boris Cherny

blocks.title: Turn uncertainty into a plan people can review

steps.title: Start with a rough proposal
steps.text: Identify the main systems and options.

steps.title: Make alternatives concrete
steps.text: Use independent designs when the direction is unclear.

steps.title: Compare agreement and differences
steps.text: Separate a common core from unresolved risks.

steps.title: Test the risky parts
steps.text: Use expert feedback and targeted spikes before scaling.
